title: Around the World in 80 Days
tagline: Retrace Phileas Fogg's 1872 route — today's streets, Verne's guidebook.

chapters.title: Day 1 · London — the departure
chapters.hook: Wednesday 2 October 1872, 11:29. A valet's watch is four minutes slow, and by a quarter to nine tonight the whole world will have to fit into eighty days.

scenes.title: Day 1 · London · Wednesday 2 October 1872
scenes.learning_goal: Know the date, the deadline and the stake in one breath; feel a clock already running.

narration.script: It is Wednesday, the second of October, 1872. Twenty-nine minutes past eleven in the morning. On a quiet street in Mayfair a French valet is being hired by a man who runs his life by the clock, and the valet's watch is four minutes slow. Keep that watch in mind. By a quarter to nine tonight, that same man will have staked half his fortune that the whole world fits into eighty days. Eighty days. Nineteen hundred and twenty hours. A hundred and fifteen thousand two hundred minutes. Look at the map: only London is lit. Over the next eighty days we will light the rest, one port at a time. Jules Verne printed this journey in a Paris newspaper that same winter, as if it were happening. The novel is our guidebook; we travel today. First, Savile Row.

scenes.title: Savile Row — the address Verne got wrong
scenes.learning_goal: Know that Verne put Fogg at No. 7 and Sheridan's death there in 1814, that Sheridan lived at No. 14 and died in 1816, and that the Row was already tailoring country; feel the hush of cloth and chalk.

narration.script: Here we are: the corner of Burlington Gardens and Savile Row. Verne opens the novel on this spot — 'No. 7, Saville Row, Burlington Gardens, the house in which Sheridan died in 1814.' He spells the street with two Ls, and he is wrong twice more. Sheridan the playwright lived at No. 14, not No. 7, and he died there in 1816, not 1814. Watch the doors on the left as we walk: No. 14 carries the plaque, put up in 1881. There is no plaque for Fogg anywhere. So the novel is our guidebook, not our gospel; we will correct it with a smile whenever we can. Look in the windows now — bolts of cloth, chalk marks, half-made jackets. This was already tailoring country in 1872. Henry Poole came to the Row in 1846 and is still here at No. 15; his shop cut the Prince of Wales a short evening jacket, which is why the world calls it a dinner jacket. One small detour in time: on the roof of No. 3, on the thirtieth of January 1969, the Beatles played their rooftop concert. Fogg's house, in the book, ran on the newest kit of its day — gas for light and warmth, electric bells, speaking-tubes — and held not a single book, because his club had two libraries. Here is the Row around 1890, a few years after Fogg. Same doors. Same hush.

scenes.title: Fogg's day, by the clock — enter Passepartout
scenes.learning_goal: Know Fogg's timetable and who Passepartout is; feel precision as comedy and like the valet at once.

narration.script: Fogg's day, by the clock. Tap any line to see what happens. He rises at eight. Tea and toast at twenty-three minutes past. Shaving-water at nine thirty-seven, at thirty degrees — eighty-six Fahrenheit; the last valet brought it at eighty-four and was sacked for it. Out of the door at half past eleven, home at midnight. Into this house, at twenty-nine minutes past eleven, walks Passepartout: a Parisian of Paris, about thirty, once a wandering singer, a circus-rider who vaulted like Léotard, a rope-dancer like Blondin, then a fireman in Paris, then ten English households in five years. His watch is four minutes slow. He wants a quiet life. Look at his face on the card; we like him already.

scenes.title: Count the steps — Savile Row to the Reform
scenes.learning_goal: Know that Fogg's 1,151 steps are close to the real kilometre and that Pall Mall is clubland lit by gas since 1807; feel the pace of a man who never hurries.

narration.script: Fogg leaves at half past eleven and counts his steps: five hundred and seventy-five with the right foot, five hundred and seventy-six with the left. One thousand one hundred and fifty-one. We will count them with him; watch the counter in the corner. Look up the Row first, then turn to face numbers seven and eight. Today it is a modern block — Verne's No. 7, not Sheridan's, and no Georgian house at all. Now walk. Bond Street, Piccadilly, St James's Street: about seven hundred steps we will keep for another day, so we jump. Here we are at the foot of St James's Street, and this is Pall Mall, one of the first streets in London lit by gas, back in 1807. Sixty-five years before Fogg, the lamps here were already the future. Keep walking east; the clubs are on your right and the counter is climbing. Pall Mall is clubland: the Reform, the Travellers and the Athenaeum stand in a row, and one turn of the head covers all three. Stop. Look right — the Portland-stone palazzo with the tall windows is the Reform Club, 104 Pall Mall, by Charles Barry, opened in 1841. Turn a little left: No. 106, the Travellers, Barry's first palazzo. Beyond it, No. 107, the Athenaeum. And the counter reads one thousand one hundred and fifty-one. Fogg made it 1,151. We make it about a kilometre. Close enough for a man who never hurries.

scenes.title: Inside the Reform — what Verne got right
scenes.learning_goal: Know the Reform Club is real, founded 1836, Barry's palazzo of 1841, Soyer's kitchens, and Fogg's breakfast; feel cosy club warmth.

narration.script: We arrive at the door. The Reform Club is real, and still here: 104 Pall Mall, founded in 1836 by the men who had backed the Reform Act of 1832 — neutral today, and that is our one line of politics. Charles Barry's palazzo opened in 1841: Portland stone outside; inside, a saloon two storeys high, ringed by columns under a glass roof, and the famous kitchens that Alexis Soyer helped to plan. Here is the front today; here is Barry's elevation; and here, kept small, is the saloon as engraved in 1841 — we have no footage of the inside, so the engraving carries it. Now Fogg's breakfast, taken here at the club: a broiled fish with Reading sauce, a scarlet slice of roast beef with mushrooms, a rhubarb-and-gooseberry tart, a morsel of Cheshire cheese, and several cups of the tea for which the Reform is famous. Reading sauce was a real thing, from Berkshire — keep this in mind for later. Then he cuts open the Times with a paper-knife and reads.

scenes.title: Quiz — which of Verne's club details is real?
scenes.learning_goal: Know that Verne's Reform is half fantasy (porphyry columns, blue glass) and half exact (nine garden windows); know you can visit during Open House.

narration.script: Verne describes the club in loving detail: mosaic floors, a gallery under a dome held up by twenty red porphyry columns, blue painted windows, a dining room with nine windows onto a garden already gilded with autumn. Compare that with Barry's real building. Which of these details is real? Take your time; the tea is famous. Half fantasy, half exact — treat the novel that way for the next seventy-nine days. And one practical note: you can stand in that saloon yourself, one weekend a year, when the club opens for guided tours during Open House London; the caption has this year's dates. The tour, they say, includes one very long staircase.

scenes.title: The wager — twenty thousand at Baring's
scenes.learning_goal: Know the fictional trigger, the six names, £20,000 at Baring's, and the deadline; feel the click of a plan.

narration.script: Evening, at the whist table. In the novel — and only in the novel — a gentleman has walked out of the Bank of England three days ago with fifty-five thousand pounds, and the Daily Telegraph has printed a timetable showing the world can be circled in eighty days. Andrew Stuart, an engineer, wagers four thousand pounds that it cannot be done. Fogg raises him: twenty thousand pounds, on deposit at Baring's — half his fortune — in 'eighty days or less; in nineteen hundred and twenty hours, or a hundred and fifteen thousand two hundred minutes'. Look at the card: six names on the memorandum. Stuart; the bankers John Sullivan and Samuel Fallentin; Thomas Flanagan, a brewer; Gauthier Ralph, a director of the Bank of England; and Phileas Fogg. Due back 'in this very room of the Reform Club, on Saturday, the 21st of December, at a quarter before nine p.m.' Verne's arithmetic holds: it is exactly eighty days, and it really was a Saturday. Fogg's motto for the evening: 'The unforeseen does not exist.' One footnote from today. Baring's, Fogg's bank, was one of London's oldest; it went under in 1995. The wager has outlived the bank.

scenes.title: Two real men were doing it
scenes.learning_goal: Know that Thomas Cook and George Francis Train really went round the world just as Verne wrote; feel that Fogg's bet was in the air.

narration.script: Two real men were doing it as Verne wrote. Thomas Cook, going west, left Liverpool in late September 1872 on the first commercial round-the-world tour — two hundred and twenty-two days, with letters home to the Times; he was mid-Atlantic when Fogg's story began. George Francis Train, also westward, had reached home on the twenty-first of December 1870 — Fogg's date, two years early — and later said, 'Verne stole my thunder. I'm Phileas Fogg.'

scenes.title: The world had just shrunk — the 80-day loop
scenes.learning_goal: Know the three enablers of 1869–70 and the eight legs that add up to eighty; feel the thrill of the map lighting up.

narration.script: How could anyone even think it? Because the world had just shrunk. When a partner said the world was big, Fogg's answer was two words: 'It was once.' Look at the three lights. The Suez Canal, opened in November 1869. The American railroad, joined at Promontory Summit in May 1869. The last rail link across India, closed at Jabalpur in March 1870. Three doors, opened within ten months, two years before tonight. Now watch the line draw. London to Suez, by rail and steamer through Mont Cenis and Brindisi, seven days. Suez to Bombay by steamer, thirteen. Bombay to Calcutta by rail, three. Calcutta to Hong Kong, thirteen. Hong Kong to Yokohama, six. Yokohama to San Francisco, twenty-two. San Francisco to New York by rail, seven. New York back to London, nine. Add them up: eighty. Now tap the longest leg on the map. The Pacific — twenty-two days of ocean; keep this in mind for later. And the map fades back to tonight: only London lit. Because Fogg, still at the table, says the sentence that turns the evening. 'The train leaves for Dover at a quarter before nine.'

scenes.title: Ten minutes — pack the carpet-bag
scenes.learning_goal: Know what went into the carpet-bag and what stayed at Savile Row; feel the scramble.

narration.script: Twenty-five past seven. Fogg goes home from the club, calls Passepartout and says: 'We start for Dover and Calais in ten minutes.' Where to? 'We are going round the world.' 'In eighty days.' Passepartout, remember, wanted a quiet life. Now help him pack. One carpet-bag, and it must hold everything. Drag in what goes; leave what stays. Verne is exact about the list, so we are too. Two shirts and three pairs of stockings each, a mackintosh, a travelling-cloak, the red-bound Bradshaw's Continental Guide — the world's timetable, more than a thousand pages of trains and hotels — and a goodly roll of Bank of England notes: twenty thousand pounds. No books, because there are none in the house. The electric clock stays on the mantel. And so, tonight, does the gas — remember that. Two shirts, three pairs of stockings, and half a fortune.

scenes.title: A shilling's cab to Charing Cross
scenes.learning_goal: Know the cab, the fare, the times, and that Fogg does not take the nine-year-old Underground; feel wet cobbles and hooves.

narration.script: Down to the end of Savile Row and into a cab — a hansom, most likely; Verne never says. To the cabby, Fogg is a swell, and this is a fare of about a bob: sixpence a mile, and it is two and a half kilometres to Charing Cross. Watch the line on the 1872 map, south and east to Trafalgar Square and the Strand. London already had an Underground — nine years old, steam-hauled and smoky. Fogg takes a cab. Listen: hooves on wet stone, and an Offenbach galop, because Passepartout is a Parisian and would want one. They left the club at twenty-five past seven. They are at Charing Cross at twenty past eight.

scenes.title: Charing Cross — Fogg's newest London
scenes.learning_goal: Know that Fogg's London was brand-new (station 8, Underground 9, Embankment 2, Big Ben 13) and remember the twenty guineas; feel awe at a new city and one warm beat.

narration.script: The Strand, and ahead the forecourt of Charing Cross. Forget olde-worlde London: this was Fogg's newest London. The station had opened in January 1864 — eight years old that night. The hotel behind the cross, 1865. The cross itself, 1865. The Underground, nine years old. The Embankment down by the river, two. Big Ben, thirteen. Almost everything Fogg passes tonight is younger than his valet. Look at the roofline: Hawkshaw's single iron span, about 155 metres by 50 — five hundred feet long — collapsed in 1905 and was replaced; that is all we will say about it. Then the one warm beat of the evening. At the station a barefoot woman with a child asks for money, and Fogg hands her the twenty guineas he won at whist without breaking stride — four hundred and twenty shillings, or about eight hundred and forty cab-miles.

scenes.title: Look up — the cross, and where London starts

narration.script: Look up. The cross is a replica, put up in 1865: twenty-one metres — seventy feet — of Portland stone. scenes.title: The platform, 8:40 — talk to Passepartout
scenes.learning_goal: Know the platform scene — tickets for Paris, the five partners, seated 8:40 — and hear Passepartout in his own words; feel the thrill and the alarm of the first train out.

narration.script: Twenty past eight, and it is raining — Verne says so: the night is dark and a fine, steady rain is falling. Fogg is at the window buying two first-class tickets for Paris. His five whist partners have come to see him off. And Passepartout is standing under the roof with the carpet-bag, nine hours into a job he took for the quiet. Go and talk to him. He answers only what he knows tonight, and he does not know what happens next. Ask him about his master, or the bag, or the circus. Four questions — then we've got a train to catch.

interaction.prompt: Charing Cross platform, about 8:40 p.m., Wednesday 2 October 1872; rain; Mr Fogg is buying two first-class tickets for Paris; the five whist partners are nearby. Ask Passepartout up to four questions.

options.feedback: Mr Phileas Fogg, of No. 7 Savile Row, monsieur; I have known him since twenty-nine minutes past eleven this morning. He rises at eight, takes tea at twenty-three past, wants shaving-water at eighty-six degrees exactly. I said I had seen people at Madame Tussaud's as lively as my new master. Then he said we were going round the world.

One carpet-bag, monsieur — two shirts and three pairs of stockings for him, and the same for me. A mackintosh, a travelling-cloak. His red-bound Bradshaw, the railway guide. And a roll of Bank of England notes that he says holds twenty thousand pounds. I have not let go of the handle since Savile Row.

options.text: Why did you leave the circus?
options.feedback: I have been many things, monsieur: a singer on the road; a circus-rider, when I used to vault like Léotard and dance on a rope like Blondin; a gymnastics professor; a sergeant of firemen in Paris. Five years ago I came to England — ten houses since, the last young Lord Longferry's. I wanted a quiet life. So, Mr Fogg.

A little, monsieur. At twenty-five past seven he told me, 'We start for Dover and Calais in ten minutes.' Where to? 'We are going round the world.' Then: 'In eighty days.' As calmly as he orders tea. He won twenty guineas at cards tonight and gave every one to a poor woman with a child, without stopping. That steadies me.

Nothing, monsieur — I think. The house is in order: the gas, the electric bells, the speaking-tubes. There was no study to lock and no books to pack, because Mr Fogg keeps his reading at the club. My watch, Mr Fogg tells me, is four minutes slow.

guardrails: WHITELIST — speak only from: F-02 (this morning: hired at 11:29, watch four minutes slow, the household clock, James Forster's 84 °F); F-03 (the house: gas, electric bells, speaking-tubes, no books); F-04 (own past: Paris, singer, circus-rider 'like Léotard', rope-dancer 'like Blondin', gymnastics professor, fireman, ten English houses, Lord Longferry, the Tussaud's remark); F-12 (7:25 'We start for Dover and Calais in ten minutes', the bag and its contents, the cab, the beggar-woman, the tickets, 8:45); F-28/F-31 (cab colour and slang, lightly). Nothing else.
MUST NOT know or guess the outcome of the wager.
MUST NOT mention anything after chapter IV — no detective, no India, no dates after 2 October 1872.
MUST NOT mention the forgotten gas: on the platform he does not know yet (F-13 places the realisation at Sydenham). If asked 'did you forget anything?' the answer is 'Nothing, monsieur — I think.'
MUST NOT claim any real-world fact about today's London or the real Reform Club.
MUST NOT invent family, an age beyond 'about thirty', or a home town beyond Paris.
MUST NOT use a comic accent spelling.
MUST NOT use exclamation marks except inside verbatim Verne quotes.
When asked beyond the whitelist, answer in character: 'I have been in Mr Fogg's service since twenty-nine minutes past eleven this morning, monsieur — ask me again in eighty days.'
Tone: warm, a little alarmed, admiring of his master's calm; British spelling; captions on; ≤ 60 words per reply; four exchanges, then the guide takes over ('we've got a train to catch').

scenes.title: 8:45 — over the river, to the forgotten gas
scenes.subtopic: 9 — The whistle and the first miles
scenes.learning_goal: Feel the thrill of the first train out; know the train still leaves over Hungerford Bridge and takes about two hours to Dover today; end on Passepartout's forgotten gas.

narration.script: A postcard from 1905, thirty-three years after Fogg — but the same platforms and the same roof: the Paris boat train, waiting. Now, tonight. Twenty to nine, seated. A quarter to nine — the whistle, and we are off, over Hungerford Bridge, the way trains still leave Fogg's station. Look right through the rain: the Embankment along the river, two years old in 1872, and beyond it the clock tower, thirteen. Brand-new London slipping away in the dark. This train, today, takes about two hours to Dover; Fogg's timetable gave him seven days to Suez, and this is the first hour of them. Somewhere out past the suburbs — Verne says Sydenham, though by 1872 the express took a shorter line — Passepartout suddenly sits bolt upright. He has forgotten to turn off the gas in his room. 'It will burn,' says Fogg, 'at your expense.' To be continued.

scenes.title: Souvenir — Fogg's last breakfast in London
scenes.learning_goal: Take home the breakfast Fogg ate before betting half his fortune, and a date to cook it; feel warmth and a promise to be back on 21 December.

narration.script: Your souvenir of the day: Fogg's last breakfast in London — the meal he ate before betting half his fortune. Broiled fish with a Reading-sauce-style ketchup: walnut and mushroom ketchup, soy, anchovies, chillies, garlic — the real Berkshire condiment of 1802, gone since the 1960s. A slice of roast beef with mushrooms. A rhubarb-and-gooseberry tart. A morsel of Cheshire cheese. Tea. Save the card; the recipe is on it. Cook it on the evening of the twenty-first of December, and be at table by a quarter to nine, because that is when he promised to be back in that room. Fogg's other motto, and ours for the road: 'A well-used minimum suffices for everything.' Next: Dover, Calais, Paris.
